entities.name: The Canon Law Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Canon Law Corpus encompasses the legal tradition of the Christian Church from the Apostolic Constitutions (c. 375 CE) through the Corpus Iuris Canonici (1582) and its modern successors. Its centerpiece is Gratian's Decretum (Concordia Discordantium Canonum, c. 1140), a systematic reconciliation of nearly 4,000 canonical texts — papal decretals, conciliar canons, Church Fathers, and Roman law — that became the foundation of European ecclesiastical jurisprudence.

The canon law tradition shaped marriage law, contract theory, criminal procedure, corporate law, and international law across medieval and early modern Europe, parallel to and deeply intertwined with the Roman civil law tradition. The 1917 and 1983 Codes of Canon Law codified this tradition for the modern Catholic Church.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Canon Law Corpus shaped marriage law and contract theory across medieval and early modern Europe, influencing international law and corporate governance. Its codification in the 1917 and 1983 Codes of Canon Law continues to impact Catholic Church jurisprudence.
